chapter: Capitol Records and "On the Street Where You Live"
title: Learning in London, Ontario that the record was a hit
summary: Fans in London, Ontario asked for his record hit; he bought the 78 to relearn what they had done, and disc jockeys flipped over "Rose Room" to push "On the Street", which set his later career.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: them said, "I think we made it, but I forgot what we did to it, how we played it, now." I said, "Well, let's play a couple of choruses like we used to do in the Embers." So we played it, and they said, "Well, that's all right, but that's not like the record." The next day I get up, go down to the record store, the biggest one in town, ask him, "Do you have a record in here by Jonah Jones, Muted Jazz?" They said, "No, we don't have that, man. We have the one, the 78, the Rhodes one, 'On the Street Where You Live'." I said, "Well, that's what I'm looking for. Do you mind if I take it back in the booth and listen?" He said, "No." So I took it back in the booth and I played it and it all come back to me then, because it was just the head, you know. Then I went back and got the guys and I took them down there, and then we were straight then. We started playing it then. And then when we get back, we find out this thing is selling, and what they sent out to the disc jockeys at that time was "Rose Room," but the disc jockeys always liked to have a hand in things that's going, so they turned it over and said, "On the Street is the number that should be pushed." So they played it all over Cleveland, and they was using it for a theme in different shows, in WLW in Chicago.
So that in effect set your career for the rest of your life, almost.
Yeah, almost, you know. It almost did, you know, for going this long, you know.
